entry.title: Should One User Be Able to Add Multiple Reactions on the Same Post? 🤔
entry.summary:
Should a single user be able to react multiple times on the same post? 🤔
Recently I noticed something interesting while using a developer community platform. A single user can react with multiple reaction types on the same post. For example: ❤️ Like One user can click several of these reactions on the same post. On one hand, this is nice because it allows people to express different emotions about the same content. But it also made me think about something from a user experience perspective. If one person adds multiple reactions, the reaction count increases multiple times — even though it came from the same user. For someone viewing the post, it might look like many people reacted, while in reality it could be just one person using several reactions. So I’m curious to hear the community’s perspective. • Allow multiple reactions from the same user only one reaction per user total reactions and number of unique users I’d really like to hear what other developers think about this. Do you think this behavior is good for engagement, or could it create confusion in reaction counts? I also opened a discussion in the open-source repository behind this platform to understand the community perspective: 👉 https://github.com/forem/forem/discussions/22941 Would love to hear your thoughts 👇
Give Valuable Feedback In comment.👇

entry.title: Stop sending your code to the cloud to find bugs
entry.summary:
I built FixMySlop to fix this. ** ** What Is It? FixMySlop is a free, open-source desktop app that scans your Runs 100% locally via Ollama — your code never leaves your machine No API keys, no subscriptions, no cloud Combines static analysis (Ruff + Bandit) with local LLM deep analysis Works on Windows, macOS, Linux On a deliberately bad Python file with 40+ planted issues: Static only: 42 issues found in 0.8 seconds Turbo mode: 10 critical issues in 25 seconds Deep mode: 44 issues in 16 seconds Slop Score: 100/100 💀
Issues it caught that static tools missed: Hardcoded AWS access keys and private RSA keys Plaintext password comparison (no hashing at all) Sensitive data leaking through URL parameters Missing tests across entire classes Race conditions in threading code ⚡ Turbo — fast, top 10 critical issues, ~25s per file. 🔍 Deep — full analysis, all issues, ~16s per file. # Launch GUI python main.py

entry.summary:
Every data person has the same nightmare. German client sends a CSV with semicolons, DD.MM.YYYY dates, and European number formatting. French client sends commas with DD/MM/YYYY.
